nodes.name: Sample preparation and reduction of NFO
nodes.procedure: NiFe₂O₄ (NFO) nanoparticles (≥99.5% purity) are dispersed in ethanol with sonication, then drop-cast onto a microelectromechanical system (MEMS)-based heating chip. This heating chip is sealed with another chip featuring a large electron-transparent Si₃N₄ membrane (30 nm thickness) for imaging, forming a nanoreactor. The nanoreactor is then assembled into the TEM holder and inserted into the TEM chamber. The oxide nanoparticles are initially heated to 400°C in 10% O₂/He to remove contamination. Following a reduction procedure in 10% H₂/He at 400°C, the NFO nanoparticles transform into a composition of NiFe and Fe₃O₄, as confirmed by selected area electron diffraction (SAED) analysis. The structural characterization of the synthesized NiFe-Fe₃O₄ reveals a classical SMSI state, with NiFe nanoparticles encapsulated by FeOₓ layers.

nodes.source_text: HRTEM sequence images captured at 700°C depict the interface reactions associated with LMSI. The images reveal a preferential epitaxial relationship between NiFe nanoparticles and Fe3O4 support during the dynamic process. The epitaxial NiFe-Fe3O4 interface initially forms a ledge-and-terrace configuration. Subsequently, the interface migrates through lateral propagation of atomic ledge along the NiFe-Fe3O4 interface. The interface migration process led to the layer-by-layer dissolution of the Fe3O4 along the (111) plane, preserving the continuity of the interface structure. The dissolution resembles the Mars-van Krevelen mechanism, where activated hydrogen from NiFe spills over to the interface, facilitating the release of lattice oxygen and reduction of Fe3O4. With lattice oxygen released from Fe3O4 at the interface, Fe2/3+ ions are reduced to mobilizable adatoms that can migrate across the Fe3O4 surface, capturing and activating oxygen gas molecules. The activation of oxygen gas takes place at the Fe3O4 {111} facets, away from the NiFe·Fe3O4 interface.

nodes.description: Hydrogen oxidation reaction on pure Fe3O4 at 700°C
nodes.source_text: In-situ experiments on pure Ni and Fe3O4 catalysts during hydrogen oxidation reaction reveal no comparable dynamic behavior. Additionally, sole Fe3O4 nanoparticles exhibit no catalytic activity nor LMSI effect under the same conditions.

nodes.description: Hydrogen oxidation reaction temperature-dependent study from 400°C to 800°C
nodes.source_text: The velocity of particle movement increases notably from 400°C to 600°C, reflecting a consistent trend with catalytic activity. With the reaction temperature reaching 800°C, both MS signals and the velocity of particle movement reach a steady state. A diffraction-spot-detection method is employed to track these dynamic diffraction spots, revealing a noticeable reduction in their lifespan.

nodes.source_text: The oxide nanoparticles are initially heated to 400°C in 10% O2/He to remove contamination. The structural characterization of the synthesized NiFe-Fe3O4, presented in Supplementary Fig. 5, reveals a classical SMSI state, with NiFe nanoparticles encapsulated by FeOx layers. Notably, these encapsulated layers exhibit remarkable instability in redox environments, completely retracting from the NiFe nanoparticles upon introduction of the reactant gas mixture.

nodes.evidence_snippet: Time-sequence TEM images of a NiFe-Fe₃O₄ system in Fig. 2a to h and Supplementary Movie 4 illustrate the synergistic effect between interfacial reduction and surface oxidation of Fe₃O₄.

nodes.characterization_summary: In-situ SAED patterns recorded during structural dynamics show phase transitions between NiFe and Fe₃O₄; diffraction spot lifespan decreases noticeably above 500°C, correlating with catalytic activity.
nodes.evidence_snippet: In-situ SAED pattern recorded during the structural dynamics (Fig. 3b) and corresponding peaks analysis (Fig. 3c) suggest that the observed structural dynamics arise from phase transitions between NiFe and Fe₃O₄.

nodes.characterization_summary: Quantitative optical flow method tracking shows nanoparticle movement velocity increases from 400°C to 600°C, reflecting consistent trend with catalytic activity; velocity reaches steady state at 800°C.
nodes.evidence_snippet: As shown in Fig. 3i-m, the velocity of particle movement increases notably from 400°C to 600°C, reflecting a consistent trend with catalytic activity. With the reaction temperature reaching 800°C, both MS signals and the velocity of particle movement reach a steady state.

nodes.characterization_summary: Automatic diffraction spot detection and tracking reveals noticeable reduction in lifespan of diffraction spots above 500°C, with average lifespan decreasing as temperature increases, correlating with structural dynamics.
nodes.evidence_snippet: A diffraction-spot-detection method is employed to track these dynamic diffraction spots (Supplementary Movie 11), revealing a noticeable reduction in their lifespan (Fig. 3n).

nodes.characterization_summary: DFT calculations with Hubbard U correction show exceptionally low hydrogen dissociation barrier of 0.11 eV for NiFe-Fe₃O₄ system, significantly lower than Fe₃O₄ and Fe-Fe₃O₄ systems.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The computed Gibbs free energy diagram reveals an exceptionally low hydrogen dissociation barrier of 0.11 eV for the NiFe-Fe₃O₄ system, which is significantly lower than the barriers observed for Fe₃O₄ and Fe·Fe₃O₄ systems (Supplementary Fig. 23).

nodes.characterization_summary: Neural network molecular dynamics simulations at 673 K over 20 ps demonstrate that NiFe preferentially attracts oxygen from Fe₃O₄ due to stronger oxygen affinity compared to Fe-Fe₃O₄, facilitating oxygen reverse spillover effect.
nodes.evidence_snippet: NN-MD simulations further elucidate the interface reduction mechanism, demonstrating that NiFe preferentially attracts oxygen from the Fe₃O₄ due to its stronger oxygen affinity compared to Fe·Fe₃O₄ (Fig. 4b, c, and Supplementary Fig. 24–26).

nodes.characterization_summary: Energy-dispersive X-ray analysis method is available for characterizing elemental composition and distribution of NiFe-Fe₃O₄ catalyst, but specific data are not reported in this study.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The elemental composition, as well as distribution, are studied on the microscope equipped with an energy-dispersive X-ray analyzer.

nodes.characterization_summary: Electron energy loss spectroscopy method is available for electronic structure analysis of NiFe-Fe₃O₄ catalyst, but specific data are not reported in this study.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Electron energy loss spectroscopy (EELS) is collected with a Gatan Imaging Filter (GIF) Quantum Model 1077 spectrometer.

nodes.characterization_summary: Operando environmental transmission electron microscopy reveals looping metal-support interaction (LMSI) in NiFe-Fe₃O₄ catalysts during hydrogen oxidation reaction, showing coordinated migration of NiFe nanoparticles across Fe₃O₄ support with etching and reconstruction.
nodes.evidence_snippet: When the reaction temperature exceeds 500°C, a distinctive catalytic dynamic behavior emerges, characterized by the coordinated migration of NiFe nanoparticles across the Fe₃O₄ support, accompanied by the etching and reconstruction of the support material (Supplementary Movie 1).

nodes.characterization_summary: In-situ ETEM experiments on pure Ni and Fe₃O₄ catalysts during hydrogen oxidation reaction reveal no comparable dynamic behavior to NiFe-Fe₃O₄ system, confirming synergetic interaction between NiFe nanoparticles and Fe₃O₄ support.
nodes.evidence_snippet: In contrast, in-situ experiments on pure Ni and Fe₃O₄ catalysts during hydrogen oxidation reaction reveal no comparable dynamic behavior (Supplementary Fig. 7).

nodes.characterization_summary: HRTEM images show layer-by-layer growth of Fe₃O₄ at {111} planes through step-flow growth mechanism, with monoatomic layer nucleation and lateral growth via Fe and O adatom attachment to step edges.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Upon reaction between reduced Fe adatoms and oxygen gas molecules, a monoatomic layer nucleates at the flat {111} plane of the Fe₃O₄, creating a step-terrace configuration, as marked by the red arrows in Fig. 1j. This newly formed atomic layer then grows laterally through step-flow growth with Fe and O adatoms attaching to the step edge (Fig. 1k–n).

nodes.characterization_summary: DFT calculations show that reduced Fe atoms migrate significantly more rapidly on Fe₃O₄ surface than through bulk, with low energy barrier for O₂ dissociation on Fe adatom anchored to Fe₃O₄ surface.
nodes.evidence_snippet: This migration proceeds significantly more rapidly on the surface than through the Fe₃O₄ bulk (Fig. 4d). Besides, the NiFe's superior H₂ dissociation activity enables hydrogen spillover across a broader region on the NiFe-Fe₃O₄ system.
